title: Financial Accounting and Reporting
officialDescription: The class introduces the financial reporting of public firms in the United States. It covers the basic economic concepts of assets, liabilities, stockholder’s equity, revenues, and expenses used to organize information into a standard set of financial statements. The focus is on accounting conventions, managerial judgments, and the resulting reporting prepared for external users such as stockholders and creditors. The class also explores the institutional context in which financial reports are produced.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to MBA students, others with permission. Not open to students who have passed ACCT 5182.

title: Financial Reporting I
officialDescription: An intensive study of financial accounting theory and practical applications as related to the preparation and analysis of financial statements, particularly focusing on assets, liabilities, owner's equity and income determination.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting Fundamentals Certificate students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Cost Analysis and Control
officialDescription: Managerial uses of accounting information for decision-making within the business enterprise. Decisions considered include product pricing, transfer pricing, make or buy, and capital budgeting. Formation of budgets establishing an internal control structure, performance evaluation, and cost control techniques are also discussed.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ACCT 5121; open only to MBA and MS in Supply Chain Management students. Not open for credit to students who have passed ACCT 5184.

title: Financial Reporting II
officialDescription: Continuation of an intensive study of financial accounting theory and practical applications as it relates to the preparation and analysis of financial statements, particularly focusing on pensions, bonds, leases, and intangibles. Also covered are accounting for consolidations, intercompany transfers, and multinational accounting.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting Fundamentals Certificate students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Assurance Services
officialDescription: An in-depth study of issues relevant to the public accounting profession, including legal liability and ethics, audit risk analysis, planning of audit engagements, auditor reports, and other assurance services and reports. Students will learn to think critically about issues facing the accounting profession primarily by analyzing cases and completing a number of individual and group research projects.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting Fundamentals Certificate students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Federal Income Taxation
officialDescription: A study of the fundamentals of Federal income taxation for individuals and related issues of compliance, reporting, and planning. Focuses on income and deduction recognition, character, and timing and includes the tax treatment of property, investments, compensation, retirement, and estates.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting Fundamentals Certificate students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Financial Statement Analysis and Business Valuation
officialDescription: Addresses the use of financial statements to analyze and value firms. Topics include advanced issues in accounting, earnings quality, performance measurement, cash flows, and accounting-based valuation and trading strategies.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to students enrolled in Accounting M.S., Advanced Business Certificate in Accounting Analytics, Advanced Business Certificate in Financial Reporting or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Ethics and the Accounting Professional Environment
officialDescription: The groundwork for fundamental issues that are included in the curriculum in the M.S. in Accounting Program relating to content and skills associated with professional success will be set.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. students or by special permission from department or unit.

title: Business Sustainability Reporting and Analysis
officialDescription: This course provides a critical analysis of current practices in business sustainability reporting and analysis. Topics covered include reporting practices, reporting frameworks, reporting standards, current and proposed regulatory requirements, rating agencies, investment products, and assurance of the reliability of the information. The course also analyzes guidance for synthesizing information from corporate sustainability disclosures into traditional financial and valuation analyses.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. and Advanced Business Certificate in Financial Reporting students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Contemporary Issues in Financial Reporting and Analysis
officialDescription: Focuses on major financial reporting issues in consideration of the current data-centric technological and analytical environment. Broad topics are derived from FASB's conceptual framework, including income determination and asset valuation. Specific topics covered include risk management, earnings management, firm valuation, investing, and corporate governance issues. Introduces tools that link non-financial metrics with financial reports, providing actionable insights for external decision makers.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S., Advanced Business Certificate in Accounting Analytics, Advanced Business Certificate in Financial Reporting students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Contemporary Managerial Accounting Issues
officialDescription: Study of major managerial accounting issues including analysis and evaluation of cost management systems. Overall focus is on the use of internally generated accounting data to support business strategy and maintain competitive advantages. Current research in the constantly evolving area of managerial accounting is emphasized.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Global Financial Reporting and Analysis
officialDescription: Students will develop and test expectations about the content of financial reports based on an understanding of how national culture and subcultures affect financial reporting in a principles-based decision environment.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. and Advanced Business Certificate in Financial Reporting students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Advanced Assurance Services
officialDescription: Advanced treatment of significant assurance services issues. Intended for students with previous coursework in assurance services and/or auditing. The course demonstrates more detailed level of audit techniques: audit planning, risk analysis, assessing internal control, executing audit procedures to substantiate validity of key financial accounts, and a presenting the audit findings in a final audit report.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. and Advanced Business Certificate in Financial Reporting students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Business Law, Business Ethics, and Public Accounting
officialDescription: Covers the major legal and ethical issues in business and their significance for the accounting profession and related stakeholders. Included among the topics are the tension between profit and the public interest, corporate responsibility to society, environmental concerns, consumer and employee relations, confidentiality, whistle blowing, advertising and hiring practices.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: This course may not be taken by MBA students, who should instead take BLAW 5175; open only to Accounting M.S. students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Forensic Accounting and Fraud Examination
officialDescription: Develops a foundation upon which forensic accounting engagements are performed. Highlighting the many contexts within which forensic accounting can be performed, students learn the roles forensic accountants play within a wide range of engagements. Students will build their forensic accounting mindset and skill set through the readings and interactions with the professor, while working on a forensic accounting engagement from inception through successful resolution.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Accounting and Disclosure for Not for Profit Entities
officialDescription: Accounting for not-for-profit organizations (NFPs), including educational institutions, hospitals and other health care entities, and civic and cultural organizations, is substantially different than for-profit entities. Examines topics relating to preparing and using financial statements for NFPs, including accounting, audit, and disclosure requirements and selected issues relating to government grants awarded to NFPs.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. and Advanced Business Certificate in Financial Reporting students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Data Analytics: Skills for Accountants
officialDescription: Introduction to the skills and technologies used to analyze data with an emphasis on preparing accountants to interact with data scientists and others. The role of data analysis in the accounting profession will be explored.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. and Advanced Business Certificate in Accounting Analytics students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Data Analytics: Accounting Applications
officialDescription: Covers practical issues such as dealing with errors in data and preparing accounting data for analysis. Additional techniques for dealing with data anomalies are explored. This technical, hands-on course prepares students for entry level accounting data analysis.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. and Advanced Business Certificate in Accounting Analytics students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Advanced Accounting Information Systems
officialDescription: An overview of Accounting Information Systems with emphasis on business process analysis, data modeling, business analytics, and internal controls. Highlights emerging trends in data analytics and its growing impact in accounting. Students work directly with various software tools to learn relational database design, data retrieval, and analysis. Introduces principles of Big Data, data visualization and software for fraud detection and internal controls.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. and Advanced Business Certificate in Accounting Analytics students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Accounting and Auditing for Governmental Entities
officialDescription: Provides students with an understanding of how the characteristics and unique objectives of government entities are manifested in the accounting standards, audit risk and disclosure requirements. Topics addressed include the purpose of the various governmental financial statements, basis of accounting, measurement, audit focus, risk, fund types, and financial statement disclosures.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. and Advanced Business Certificate in Financial Reporting students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Enterprise Risk Management: Identify Events as Risks to Manage or Opportunities to Seize
officialDescription: Provides students with the ability within the COSO framework to identify events that may impact a nonfinancial publicly traded enterprise's ability to realize value for its stakeholders using the concept of the triple bottom line of profit, people, and planet. Events will be evaluated as risks that have negative impacts and opportunities as well as potential positive impacts. ERM techniques applied in the course will include: risk control, business continuity, reputation risk, supply-chain management, compensation system alignment, and strategic decisions.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Taxation of Business Entities - Flow Through Entities
officialDescription: Application of basic tax concepts to business entities, with particular emphasis on flow through entities. At the end of the course, students should be able to identify and address the tax issues faced when forming, operating, and liquidating a flow through entity.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. and Advanced Business Certificate in Taxation students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Taxation of Business Entities: C Corporations
officialDescription: Application of basic tax concepts to business entities, with particular emphasis on C corporations. At the end of the course, students should be able to identify and address the tax issues faced when forming, operating, and liquidating a C corporation.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. and Advanced Business Certificate in Taxation students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Taxes and Business Strategy
officialDescription: Provides a foundation for understanding how taxes affect economic behavior. Students work through a conceptual framework that describes how tax rules affect business decisions. At the end of this course, students should be able to apply this conceptual framework to a number of settings including compensation, organizational form, investment strategies, and multinational tax issues.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. and Advanced Business Certificate in Taxation students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Research for Accounting Professionals
officialDescription: This course provides students with the information literacy skills required of an accounting professional to identify information needs, specify and implement research strategies, evaluate resources in order to fulfill those needs, and communicate findings.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. and Advanced Business Certificate in Taxation students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Financial Reporting of Income Taxes
officialDescription: Focuses on the financial reporting provisions related to federal, foreign, and state income taxes. Students will learn how to calculate income tax amounts reported on the income statement and balance sheet and prepare the income tax footnote and related disclosures.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S., Advanced Business Certificate in Taxation, Advanced Business Certificate in Financial Reporting students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Advanced Accounting
officialDescription: An in-depth study of accounting for business combinations. Coverage also includes contemporary issues in financial accounting, such as multinational entities and partnerships.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S. students or by special permission from the department or unit. Not open to students who have passed ACCT 4203.

title: Special Topics in Accounting
officialDescription: Investigation and discussion of special topics in accounting. May be repeated for a total of nine credits.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Accounting M.S., Advanced Business Certificate in Taxation, Advanced Business Certificate in Financial Reporting students or by special permission from the department or unit.

title: Independent Study in Accounting
officialDescription: Faculty-student interaction on a one-to-one basis involving independent study of specific areas of accounting. Emphasis, selected by the student, may be on theoretical or applied aspects. A written report is required.

title: Introduction to Accounting Research
officialDescription: This seminar introduces students to three major elements of accounting research: research validity, with an emphasis on examples in accounting research; paradigms used in accounting research; and basic research design issues and how those issues are illustrated in the accounting literature. Finally, students will be exposed to data sources and analysis with commonly used statistical software.

title: Accounting and Capital Markets
officialDescription: Provides a broad survey of capital markets research in accounting and related fields. Students are introduced to major theoretical and methodological issues in this line of research. The seminar focuses on theoretical and intuitive constructs that frame accounting research questions and the methods that are used to address those research questions.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Instructor consent.

title: Archival Audit Research
officialDescription: Provides a broad overview of archival, empirical research in auditing and audit markets. Students are introduced to the major theoretical and methodological issues in this section of research. Topics covered include: audit quality, the supply of/market for auditing, the demand for/value of auditing, internal control, audit committees, audit regulation, and audit opinions.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Instructor consent.

title: Research in Taxation
officialDescription: This seminar provides a broad survey of research in taxation. Students are introduced to the major theoretical and methodological issues in this line of research. The seminar focuses on theoretical and intuitive constructs that frame tax research questions and the methods and data that are used to address those research questions.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Instructor consent.

title: Seminar in Special Research Topics
officialDescription: Students are exposed to a broad range of accounting research through reading and critiquing research papers presented at the Accounting Department Research Workshop (papers are presented by local scholars as well as scholars from other institutions). The seminar also focuses on how to present effective written and oral criticisms of research papers.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Instructor consent.

title: Racial Justice and Decoloniality in Higher Education Teaching
officialDescription: (Also offered as EDLR 6470, LLAS 6470.) Theory and practice of how teaching within a higher education context can work toward racially equitable learning experiences and decoloniality of the classroom.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Recommended preparation: EDLR 5201, 6467; GRAD 6000, 6001.

title: Biostatistics for Health Professions
officialDescription: Basic statistical methods in a broad range of medical or public health problems. Emphasizes the use of these methods and the interpretation of results using biomedical and health sciences applications.

title: Investigation of Special Topics
officialDescription: Advanced topics and investigations in the field of Allied Health Sciences. Topics and credits to be published prior to the registration period preceding the semester offering.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Instructor consent.

title: Independent Study for Allied Health
officialDescription: Advanced study, project, or research of intensive, independent investigation in allied health consistent with the student's needs, interests and plan of study.

title: Behavioral Intervention Development and Evaluation
officialDescription: Examines the history and purpose of behavioral interventions, how to develop behavioral interventions, conceptual models, study designs to test behavioral interventions, and methodological challenges in behavioral intervention research. Students will learn how to design conceptually sound behavioral interventions, how to design scientifically sound trials to test them, and how to critically evaluate published behavioral trials.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: A course in research methods such as AH 4239, AH 4241, or AH 6306, or as approved by instructor. Instructor consent required.

title: HAZWOPER
officialDescription: Provides individuals the necessary knowledge and training to meet the criteria for certification recognized by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) in work activities related to hazardous waste sites and cleanup operations involving hazardous substances. Optional field exercise. Only students who successfully complete both the academic and hands-on field exercise offered within this course will receive a 40-hour HAZWOPER certificate.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Not open to students who have successfully completed AH 3275.

title: Professional Development Project
officialDescription: Examines contemporary issues and problems relevant to allied health practice. Focus is on interdisciplinary exchange of ideas and the development of a project relative to the student's particular program emphasis.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: At least nine credits in Allied Health courses; open only to non-thesis (Plan B) students; instructor consent required.

title: Professional Development Practicum
officialDescription: The implementation and/or application of theory in AH 5314. A minimum of 300 practicum hours required.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: AH 5314, which may be taken concurrently; open only to non-thesis (Plan B) students; instructor consent required.

title: Health Education and Behavioral Interventions for At-Risk Populations
officialDescription: The study and application of current learning theories, models, and strategies used by experienced health professionals to become effective interventionists within didactic, clinical, and community settings.

title: Italy's Mediterranean Food and Our Health
officialDescription: Production and processing of the characteristic foods of Italy. Summary of the Italian Mediterranean diet: definitions, culture, history, food consumption patterns, nutrient composition and potential health benefits. Emphasis on the difference in diet between Italians and Americans in relation to the health differences between the two populations. May not be counted toward the Allied Health Sciences major's group A or science elective requirements. Taught with AH 2330.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to NUSC and DIET majors, others by consent of instructor. Not open for credit if previously passed AH 2330.

title: Community Nutrition Education and Behavioral Intervention Delivery for At-Risk Groups
officialDescription: Community nutrition experiences with income-challenged individuals and families aligned with the model of health promotion sciences and towards achieving entry-level competence in community nutrition and public health.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Students must earn a “C” or higher in DIET 3215, 3231W, 3235, 3250, 3272, and NUSC 3230 or equivalents.

title: Advanced Medical Nutrition Therapy
officialDescription: Provides student with advanced nutrition therapy information for the effective treatment of complex medical problems. Emphasizes all aspects of the nutrition care process as it relates to medical conditions. The research regarding the physiological, pathological and metabolic basis for nutrient modifications will be emphasized.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Dietetics majors, others by consent of the Director of Dietetics.

title: Contemporary Nutrition Issues and Research
officialDescription: Critical thinking and application of research to contemporary issues in food and nutrition applied to clinical nutrition and community/public health nutrition. Learning occurs through classroom discussions, self-exploration through reading and applying scientific studies to issues, and participation in a research project.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to Dietetics majors, others by consent of the Director of Dietetics.

title: Environmental Health
officialDescription: Focuses on the environmental health consequences of exposure to toxic chemicals, food contaminants and radiation. Basic principles of environmental health are discussed, followed by lectures on specific topics such as: cancer and reproductive risks, occupational hazards, radiation, genetic biomontoring, risk assessment techniques, risk/benefit analysis, social/legal aspects of regulating toxic chemicals, and other related topics.

title: Applied Advanced Nutrition
officialDescription: Provides student with advanced nutrition information for the effective management of complex medical and public health problems. Emphasizes the impact of nutrients and food components on human health. The research regarding the physiological, pathological and metabolic basis for nutrients in health and disease will be emphasized.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: DIET 4272, 4350, 4360 and 4365 or equivalent.

title: Health Promotion through Foodservice: Advanced Management Practicum I
officialDescription: Supervised practice experiences in food service settings to promote health and wellbeing through delivery of healthy, safe, culinarily pleasing food which meets budgetary constraints with efficiency. Culminating project utilizing project management skills by implementing a healthy cooking class involving planning and scheduling, marketing, healthy menu development, teaching, budgetary needs and cost control, continuous quality improvement, and program evaluation.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Student must earn a "C" or better in DIET 3150, 3155; open only to Dietetics majors, others by consent of Dietetics Program Director.

title: Seminar in Dietetics
officialDescription: Interactive graduate seminar addressing contemporary issues in dietetics through observation, stakeholder engagement, and continuous quality improvement. Students will develop management, mentoring, and advocacy skills, explore reimbursement systems, examine emerging nutrition trends, and refine leadership and negotiation competencies for effective professional practice.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Instructor consent required. Not open for credit to students who have passed DIET 4470 when offered as "Seminar in Dietetics."

title: Poverty and Public Health
officialDescription: Social determinants of health and poverty. Health impact assessments. Improving the social determinants of health and poverty, including countries in conflict.

title: Health Equity and Social Determinants of Health
officialDescription: This course will apply action frameworks targeting structural, social, and intermediary determinants of physical and mental health inequities with the goal of eliminating inequities in health.

title: Vaccines: Mechanisms of Immune Protection
officialDescription: (Also offered as PATH 5632.) Focuses on several different approaches to inducing prophylactic immunity in the host. Both traditional and modern molecular approaches to vaccine design will be discussed. In addition, the mechanisms employed by pathogenic microbes to avoid hosts' immune responses will be examined in the context of vaccine design. The students will gain an appreciation for the transition from basic research to practical applications.

title: Theory and Practice of Clinical Genomics
officialDescription: Theory and practice of diagnostic laboratory methodologies and genomic data analyses for the clinical scientist. Sections are taught in a series of modules and include clinical case scenarios and analyses. With a change of content, this course may be repeated for credit.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Instructor consent. Recommended preparation: A course in human genetics.

title: Multilevel Mediation-Moderation Modeling for Health Sciences
officialDescription: Presents advanced multivariate statistical methods focusing on statistical techniques commonly used in empirical research under a latent-variable approach teaches students multilevel mediation-moderation techniques in order to analyze complex or multilevel databases. At the end of the course, students will understand how to analyze multivariate data using multilevel mediation-moderation concepts to test a variety of health-related research hypotheses. Knowledge of linear models is needed for participants enrolling in this course.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: A course in precalculus or higher; AH 5005 or other advanced/graduate course in statistics.

title: Analysis of Large Population-Based Datasets for Health Promotion
officialDescription: Methods for using large population-based health-related datasets for health promotion research. Topics include procedures for accessing data, strengths and limitations of these data for health promotion research, complex sampling and weighted statistical analyses, and interpretation and communication of findings.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: AH 3005, AH 5005, or equivalent biostatistics course and familiarity with statistical analysis software (e.g., SAS, Stata, R, SPSS); instructor consent required.

title: Experiential Learning in Health Promotion Research
officialDescription: Mentored research experiences on and/or off-campus to increase doctoral student's breadth and depth of knowledge, skills and competence in health promotion science.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: AH 6324; a graduate statistics course; instructor consent required; open only to doctoral students after first semester of doctoral work.

title: Graduate Seminar in Health Promotion Research
officialDescription: In a small learning environment under the direction of one or more faculty, students develop their research and academic abilities in health promotion sciences. Activities include: individual goal setting and implementing learning plans; attending scientific seminars; preparing and delivering research presentations; research writing; college-level teaching; grant and compliance administration; and applying for post-graduate employment.

title: Program Planning and Evaluation for Health Professionals
officialDescription: A theoretical and practical introduction to program evaluation for health professionals who deliver health care services, manage departments and personnel, or provide training and continuing educational opportunities. Students apply the practical program evaluation framework for health-related intervention programs and document the impact of interventions within health promotion and disease and disability prevention programs. Skill development is facilitated.

title: Research Methods in Allied Health
officialDescription: An inquiry into the nature of research with emphasis on the spirit, logic, and components of the scientific method. Health related research literature is used to aid the student in learning to read, understand, and critically analyze published materials. The preparation of research proposals and reports is emphasized.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: EPSY 5605 or a course in basic statistics.

title: Introduction to Systems Science and Complexity
officialDescription: An introduction to the basic concepts and characteristics of complex systems, as well as useful tools to study complex behavioral and social systems (with examples in health), such as social network analysis, system dynamics modeling and agent-based modeling.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Pre-calculus or higher, and statistics covering topics including regression analysis; instructor consent required.

title: Critical Issues in Health Promotion, Disease and Disability Prevention
officialDescription: An in-depth study of health promotion, disease and disability prevention policies, programs and strategies.

title: Writing Scientific Grant Proposals and Papers
officialDescription: Designed for advanced graduate student in a health field to obtain experience writing a scientific research proposal. Students will be expected to enter the course with both a fairly well developed research topic and an actual Request for Proposal in hand. The final outcome from this class will be a grant proposal that is suitable for submission to a funding agency.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Instructor consent.

title: Special Topics
officialDescription: Topics relating to the College of Agriculture, Health and Natural Resources.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Instructor consent.

title: Independent Study in Extension
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Instructor consent.

title: Leadership Development
officialDescription: Introduction to extension, outreach education and other forms of public engagement (governmental and nongovernmental). For students interested in a career in or knowing about outreach education and public engagement.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to students in the College of Agriculture, Health and Natural Resources, others with instructor consent.

title: Foundations of Applied Linguistics and Discourse Studies
officialDescription: Issues in applied linguistics such as second language learning and teaching, curriculum development, language assessment and program evaluation, sociolinguistics, technological application in language learning and teaching, discourse analysis, and cognitive approaches to applied linguistics.

title: Developing Pragmatic Competence in Another Language: Research and Practice
officialDescription: An introduction to pragmatics in second language acquisition with emphasis on research and practice in the teaching and learning of a second language.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to graduate students in LCL, others with instructor consent.

title: Applied Cognitive Linguistics
officialDescription: Introduction to cognitive linguistics with emphasis on its application to the creation of multimodal texts and the teaching and learning of a second language.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to graduate students in LCL, others with instructor consent.

title: Teaching for Intercultural Citizenship and Human Rights I
officialDescription: (Also offered as CLCS 5324, GERM 5324.) Explores the role of intercultural competence and human rights education from a variety of perspectives, including applied linguistics, education, psychology, neuroscience, philosophy, and pragmatics. Through readings, online and face-to-face discussions, role-plays, scenarios, and presentations students will critically reflect on models of intercultural competence and human rights education and their relation to (student) outcomes; examine the role of social justice and human rights within the teaching of intercultural competence; and integrate and assess intercultural competence in teaching. Taught in English.

title: Teaching for Intercultural Citizenship and Human Rights II
officialDescription: (Also offered as CLCS 5325, GERM 5325.) Continued exploration of the role of intercultural competence and human rights education from a variety of perspectives, including applied linguistics, education, psychology, neuroscience, philosophy and pragmatics. Students will design a research project or curricular unit for a specific purpose in which they apply models of intercultural competence/ citizenship and human rights in practice. Taught in English.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ALDS 5324 or CLCS 5324 or GERM 5324 or instructor consent.

title: Variable Topics
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Prerequisites and recommended preparation vary.

title: Engineering Analysis
officialDescription: Advanced math topics including Laplace, Fourier and z-Transform methods, probability theory, ordinary differential equations and systems of ODEs, partial differential equations, vector calculus, elements of statistics, linear and non-linear optimization, matrix theory, and special functions like Bessel, Legendre, and gamma. This course is set up as modules. Students will be required to complete certain modules depending on their background and concentrations.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to graduate students only.

title: Computer Aided Engineering
officialDescription: Introduction to computational methods in design and analysis of materials, processes, and systems related to advanced manufacturing and energy systems. Topics covered include computational materials, process simulation, computational fluid dynamics, finite element analysis, and manufacturing process simulation.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to graduate students only.

title: Engineering Communication
officialDescription: Development of the advanced communication skills as well as the information management required of engineers and engineering managers in industry, government and business. Focus on the design and writing of technical reports, articles, proposals, and the memoranda that address the needs of diverse organizational and professional audiences; the preparation and delivery of organizational and technical oral and multimedia presentations and briefings; team building skills with an emphasis on communications; and knowledge management.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to graduate students only.

title: Special Topics in Advanced Manufacturing for Energy Systems
officialDescription: Classroom and/or laboratory courses in special topics as announced in advance for each semester. The field of study or investigation is to be approved by the Program Director before announcement of the course.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Instructor consent.

title: American Studies: Methods and Major Texts
officialDescription: (Also offered as ENGL 6800, HIST 6000.) Introduction to the methodologies and topics of American Studies through a survey of major texts in the field, past and present. Course also provides a history of the field.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to graduate students in English, History, and Political Science; open to others with consent.

title: American Studies: Keywords
officialDescription: (Also offered as ENGL 6850, HIST 6850.) Detailed study of a specific topic in American cultural studies with an emphasis on developing skills in interdisciplinary research. Topics vary from semester to semester.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to graduate students in English, History, and Political Science; open to others with consent.

title: Graduate Professional Development I: Academic Writing Tools
officialDescription: This course introduces students to graduate-level scientific writing, including the elements of a scientific paper, formatting, and references. Scientific paper reading, reviewing, and note-taking with a focus on preparing literature reviews and conference-style abstracts will be highlighted.

title: Graduate Professional Development: Communication, Teaching, and Digital Presence
officialDescription: This course develops advanced professional communication and digital identity skills for graduate students in the animal and biological sciences. Students learn to communicate their research effectively through oral presentations, poster design, and creation of an authentic digital professional presence. In addition, they will be introduced to the basics of pedagogy with a focus on different instruction modalities including in-class and online instruction. The course culminates in a short “About Me” video project suitable for sharing on LinkedIn, a lab website, or other online platforms. Peer feedback and reflection guide students toward clear, confident, and professional self-presentation.

title: Introduction to Data Analysis in Agriculture
officialDescription: Concepts of data analysis applied to agriculture. Introduction to R/Rstudio and basic elements of coding, data management, data cleaning, graphics, and statistical analysis. The course covers software installation, basic and intermediate usage, and some of the common data analysis tools used in agricultural research. Additionally, the course covers some basic examples of bioinformatics that are commonly used in agriculture. Course includes recorded lectures, notes, homework, two small data analysis projects, and a capstone data analysis project.

title: Food Microbiology and Safety
officialDescription: Microorganisms associated with food, including their roles in fermentation, spoilage, and foodborne illness. Principles and applications of food preservation, pathogen detection, and strategies to enhance food safety and quality. Graduate students will participate in guided discussion sessions with the instructor to develop a scientific review paper on a current topic in food microbiology and safety, integrating primary literature and evidence-based analysis. Taught concurrently with ANSC 4341.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Recommended preparation: A background in general microbiology or concurrent registration in a microbiology course.

title: Experimental Design in Animal Science
officialDescription: Discussion of the basic principles of design and analysis for experiments in animal and food science. Both theory and practical application of designing experiments will be included. Emphasis is placed on data analysis using SAS, highlighting determination of the most appropriate analysis for an experiment and interpretation of output.

title: Growth and Metabolism of Domestic Animals
officialDescription: An assessment of animal growth and metabolism interrelated to nutrition, selection, environment, production and idiosyncrasies among species.

title: Advanced Animal Nutrition
officialDescription: A comparative study of nutritional, physiological, microbiological, immunological and biochemical aspects of digestion and metabolism in the non-ruminant and ruminant animal. Topics include digestive system structures, utilization of nutrients, energy metabolism, control of nutrient metabolism, and experimental techniques used in the study of animal nutrition. Feedstuffs appropriate to meet nutrient requirements and ration formulation across various physiological stages, growth, gestation, and lactation will be covered in this course. There will be a focus on developing critical thinking skills, reading current literature, and assimilating scientific concepts in written and oral forms.

title: Comparative Exercise Physiology
officialDescription: In depth discussion of the effects of exercise on the body with emphasis placed on the physiological mechanisms which allow for adaptation to periods of exercise and inactivity. Idiosyncrasies among the athletic species will be highlighted.

title: Endocrinology of Farm Animals
officialDescription: In depth discussion on endocrine systems and endocrine function in farm animals with emphasis on hormones involved in metabolism, growth, lactation, feed intake and digestion in cattle, pigs, horses and poultry.

title: Probiotics and Prebiotics
officialDescription: Explores the biology, mechanisms, efficacy, and safety of probiotics and prebiotics, emphasizing the microbiome’s role in health and disease and the molecular mechanisms underlying their health benefits. Students critically evaluate commercial products and functional foods containing probiotics and prebiotics using scientific literature to develop evidence-based conclusions. Diverse assessments including papers, presentations, brochures and infographics support varied learning styles and foster NACE competencies in critical thinking, communication, and professionalism. A background in microbiology is recommended.

title: Signaling Pathways
officialDescription: Principles of cell signaling transduction. Major cellular regulatory pathways and interactions between pathway components. Regulatory mechanism of various cellular processes via specific signaling network, and methods used for studying cell-signaling pathways.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Recommended preparation: Previous three-credit course in cell biology, molecular biology, or biochemistry.

title: Frontiers in Animal Embryo Biotechnology
officialDescription: Focuses on the epigenetics and molecular aspects of embryology such as genomic imprinting and X inactivation. Introduces the state of numerous established and emerging embryo biotechnologies such as assisted reproductive technologies; gamete cryopreservation; transgenesis; nuclear transfer (cloning); gene targeting/genome editing; xenotransplantation; embryonic and tissue stem cells, induced pluripotent stem cells and their applications.

title: Animal Food Products: Dairy Technology
officialDescription: Production and processing of milk and milk products from a food science perspective, including chemical, physical, and microbiological components. Technological aspects of the transformation of milk into various food products. Public health regulations, good manufacturing practices, cleaning and sanitizing procedures. Unit operations in dairy food manufacturing, packaging, labeling, and quality control procedures.

title: Food Chemistry
officialDescription: Chemical, physical and biological changes in foods and food macromolecules that occur during processing and storage that affect texture, color, flavor, stability and nutritive qualities. Field trips may be required.

title: Muscle Biology and Muscle Food Chemistry
officialDescription: Molecular and cellular basis of muscle food physical features and its related muscle biological events.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to graduate students. Recommended Preparation: ANCS 3343 or CHEM 2241 or CHEM 2443 or one same-level chemistry class.

title: Research
officialDescription: Independent research in animal science, livestock production, meats, dairy production, animal nutrition, growth, reproductive physiology, animal breeding, or environmental health.

title: Graduate Presentation Skills
officialDescription: A discussion-based class that prepares students to make oral presentations.

title: Animal Science Seminar
officialDescription: Students present a seminar on the topic of their thesis research.

title: Special Topics in Animal Science
officialDescription: May be repeated for credit with a change of topic.

title: Human Behavioral Ecology
officialDescription: Applies the theory of natural selection to the study of human behavior in an ecological setting, with particular focus on the adaptive features and biological design of human behavior.

title: Human Evolutionary Theory
officialDescription: Evolutionary concepts applied to human body size and shape, diet, disease, group composition, and reproductive behavior.

title: History of Anthropological Theory
officialDescription: Development of theory from the nineteenth century through the 1970s. Required for graduate students in Cultural and Historical Anthropology.

title: Seminar: Contemporary Theory in Social and Cultural Anthropology
officialDescription: Selected current issues and debates in the discipline.

title: Decolonial Alternatives: Sense Making, Political Practices and Collective Experiences
officialDescription: Covers a wide-range of debates around decoloniality, including liberation and anti-colonial struggles, Indigenous epistemologies, black liberation, pluriversal proposals and multi-species justice.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to advanced undergraduates with permission of the instructor.

title: Gender and Culture
officialDescription: (Also offered as WGSS 5315.) Anthropological perspectives on the analysis of gender with special focus on dynamics of gender, culture, and power.

title: Environmental Anthropology
officialDescription: Examines the theories and methods of environmental anthropology and its application to contemporary human-environmental problems including climate change, environmental degradation, and environmental injustice.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Recommended preparation: Strong background in the one or more of the four fields of anthropology.

title: Ethnographic Methods I
officialDescription: Theoretical foundations and basic tools used to conduct professional field studies in anthropology. Research design; moral and ethical dimensions of field work; designing and conducting informal, semi-structured and structured interviews (one-on-one and in groups); managing field notes, questionnaires, and data; computer data management; summary statistics and graphics; identifying and interpreting random variation; modeling and testing explanations.

title: Propaganda, Disinformation, and Hate Speech
officialDescription: (Also offered as HRTS 5327.) Draws on current social science research and legal scholarship to understand the effects of disinformation and hate speech on individual moral decision-making, as well as on wider politics and culture. Evaluates various private and public initiatives to regulate speech.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Not open for credit to students who have passed ANTH/HRTS 3230.

title: Cognitive Science of Religion
officialDescription: Theoretical debates and methodological approaches to the cognitive and evolutionary study of religious thought and behavior. Key topics include religious transmission, theological incorrectness, magical thinking, and psychosocial functions of religion and ritual.

title: Cognitive Anthropology
officialDescription: Study of how the content of thought or knowledge, is created, organized, and distributed in human communities. Topics include cultural models of the mind, emotions, personality, and relationships.

title: Culture and Religion
officialDescription: Theories and problems in the analysis of non-western religious systems.

title: Analysis of Rituals
officialDescription: Examines various theoretical contributions to the anthropological study of ritual. Controversies and ambiguities surrounding the social and symbolic significance of the ritual act for both men's and women's experiences and participation are addressed.

title: The Neanderthals
officialDescription: Biological, cultural, technological, and behavioral evolution of Neanderthals as understood through the fields of genetics, physical anthropology, palaeolithic archaeology, human behavioral ecology, hunter-gatherer ethnography, palaeoclimatology, chronometric dating, and geology. Neanderthal-Modern Human interactions and the Middle-Upper Palaeolithic transition are also considered.

title: Medical Anthropology
officialDescription: Overview of current theory and practice in medical anthropology.

title: Multimodal and Community Engaged Research
officialDescription: Overview of multimodal, applied, public-facing, and community engaged approaches to humanistic social science research. Emphasis upon the ethics and politics of collaboration and multi-media forms of scholarship (video, sound, design, performance, etc.).

title: History of Archaeological Theory
officialDescription: A critical review of the development of archaeology, with particular emphasis on the theoretical innovations of the 1960s and 1970s.

title: Archaeological Site Formation Processes
officialDescription: Creation of archaeological sites by human behavior and geological forces. The characteristics of various formation processes and identification of them in the archaeological record.

title: Race, Racialization, and Health
officialDescription: A transdisciplinary approach to understanding racialization as a process and tool that is inextricable from the formation and continuation of medicine and public health. Through a critical medical anthropology lens, students will engage with studies of race science, medical racism, medical experimentation, genomics and epigenetics, and structural violence in/of health care and public health to examine how capitalism, international health and medical markets, governments, colonialism, and im/migration shape the ways that disease burden and differential access to healthcare are distributed across populations.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Prior coursework in medical anthropology required for undergraduates.

title: Global Health and Anthropology
officialDescription: Assessing global morbidity and mortality; global health governance; political economy of global health; health inequities; social determinants of health; syndemics; climate change and health; maternal and child health; nutrition; infectious diseases; and war, trauma, and complex emergencies.

title: Special Topics
officialDescription: Special topic readings or investigations according to the needs of each student.

title: Variable Topics
officialDescription: With a change in content, may be repeated for credit.

title: Introduction to Stable Isotopes
officialDescription: Introduction to stable isotope theory, methodology, and applications.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to graduate students only.

title: Paleoclimate Reconstruction
officialDescription: The impact of past climate on human societies, from Mid-Pleistocene to late Holocene, discussed in light of modern climatology and paleoclimate reconstruction methods.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to graduate students only.

title: Professional Development in Anthropology
officialDescription: Hands-on survey of practical skills required for professional anthropology, including writing research plans, grant applications, manuscript preparation, teaching philosophies, professional behavior and ethics.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to graduate students in Anthropology, others with consent.

title: Modern Human Dispersals
officialDescription: Interdisciplinary understanding of the tempo and mode of modern human dispersals across Europe, Asia, Australia, and the Americas.

title: Hunter-Gatherers Past and Present
officialDescription: Investigation of recent and prehistoric hunter-gatherer societies informed by human behavioral ecology, archaeology, and ethnoarchaeology.

title: Quantitative Zooarchaeology
officialDescription: Archaeological problem solving using zooarchaeological and taphonomic data; the evolutionary ecology of human economies; evaluation and quantification of zooarchaeological data; formation of faunal assemblages.

title: Archaeobotany
officialDescription: Method and theory of studying archaeological plant remains in the laboratory, including sampling, identification, and interpretation of data.

title: Plants and People Through the Ages
officialDescription: Survey of the dynamic relationship between plants and people using an inter-disciplinary approach. Readings draw from anthropology, archaeology, botany, ecology, history, and agricultural and environmental sciences.

title: Race, Gender, and Science
officialDescription: (Also offered as LLAS 5750.) Exploration of how race, sex, and gender have been conceptualized and studied across various scientific disciplines in the past and present, and how that science both shapes and is shaped by society.

title: Race in the Formation of the Human Sciences
officialDescription: (Also offered as LLAS 5800, POLS 5800, PHIL 5800.) Exploration of how race and the human sciences emerged out of the theological, epistemological, and political upheavals that resulted in the Euromodern world.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Not open for credit to students who have passed PHIL 5380.

title: Microeconomics
officialDescription: Beginning graduate microeconomics covering consumer and producer theory, price determination, economic efficiency, and welfare analysis.

title: Economics Methodology: Praxis and Practice
officialDescription: Philosophical foundations of economics as a science and economic research. Developing skills for planning, performing, reporting, and evaluating economic research. Critical thinking about the research process, reading about and discussing research methodology, analyzing the logic and reasoning of other economists’ research articles, and developing a research project.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: M.S. student in ARE, or ARE major with Senior standing and instructor approval.

title: Market Planning and Survey Research in the Food Industry
officialDescription: Overview of market planning in the food industry, with emphasis on survey design and implementation. Graduate students will lead teams of undergraduates as they work with clients to develop tailored market plans.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 3333 or similar course. Not open for credit to students who have passed ARE 4205.

title: Data Science for Decision Making in Applied and Resource Economics
officialDescription: This course introduces data science and its transformative role in decision-making across business and policy applications in applied and resource economics. Students will learn to analyze and interpret data using R, with hands-on practice in visualization, A/B testing, regression analysis, and machine learning. Designed for beginners, it emphasizes intuitive approaches and practical applications, preparing students to apply data science in real-world contexts.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Recommended preparation: Statistics, such as STAT 1000Q or STAT 1100Q or a similar course. Not open for credit to students who have passed ARE 4210.

title: Sustainable Business Planning
officialDescription: The practice of creating a sustainable business plan as a critical step for entrepreneurial success. In this course you will learn principles of marketing, financial and human resource management as well as budgeting techniques and the legal and organizational structure of businesses while creating a sustainable business plan.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 2210 and ARE 2215 or equivalent courses in business management and accounting with instructor's consent. Not open for credit to students who have passed ARE 4215.

title: Sustainable Economic Development
officialDescription: The role of sustainable economic development of less developed economies. Microeconomic dimensions of agricultural development, food security, agricultural production and supply, foreign assistance, and government programming.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Not open for credit to students who have passed ARE 4305.

title: Applied Econometrics I: Regression Analysis for Causal Inference
officialDescription: Provides a rigorous foundation in applied econometrics with a focus on regression analysis for causal inference. Regression analysis helps address real-world problems beyond prediction, offering tools to examine causal relationships. Emphasizes both theoretical foundations—model assumptions, derivations, and identification strategies—and hands-on empirical data analysis. By the end of the course, students will be able to frame testable hypotheses, analyze complex real-world data, and apply econometric methods to inform research, policy, and data-driven business strategies.

title: Applied Econometrics II: Advanced Causal Inference
officialDescription: Econometric methods used in contemporary applied economic data analysis to examine causal relationships as well as machine learning techniques. Covered techniques include, but are not limited to, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, synthetic control methods, and causal forest. Emphasis in lecture will be placed on formulating identification strategies and implementing in standard statistical software (of the student's choosing).
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 5311 or STAT 5405 or instructor consent. Not open for credit to students who have passed ARE 6313.

title: Data Ethics and Equity in the Era of Misinformation
officialDescription: This course will introduce students to issues of ethics and equity in the contemporary practice of data science. The ability to collect, store, process, and analyze ever greater amounts of data offers great opportunities, as well as potential perils. This course will provide examine the ethical implications of data collection, usage, and distribution. Topics will include systematic approaches to assessing ethical issues; privacy and confidentiality; defining research and the responsibilities associated with conducting ethical research; implicit and structural biases in data collection and analysis.

title: Climate Economics
officialDescription: Analysis of the interactive relationship between the economy and climate change. Use of advanced principles and tools of economics to focus on the costs of changes in the severity and frequency of weather events, how these costs are influenced by markets and policies, and how costs and benefits are distributed across populations within the U.S and across the globe in the short and long terms. Examination of household, firm-level, national and international decision-making as influenced by climate change, taking into account uncertainty, diverging interests, external costs, and evaluation of models used to alternative scenarios.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: This course and ARE 3438E may not both be taken for credit.

title: Global Energy Transitions
officialDescription: Recent theoretical and empirical research on the economics of clean energy transitions from a global perspective. Topics include fossil fuel extraction, critical minerals and metals, renewable and green technologies, and challenges involved in decarbonizing electricity generation and consumption. Cross-cutting themes include energy poverty and development, industrial and climate policies, environmental impacts, and political economy. Focus on developing data-driven research and empirical estimation.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 5201 or ECON 5201 or equivalent graduate-level microeconomics course with instructor approval; ARE 5311 or ECON 5311 or equivalent graduate-level econometrics course with instructor approval. Not open for credit to students who have passed ARE 6440.

title: Environmental and Resource Economics
officialDescription: Natural resource use and environmental quality analysis using economic theory. Reviews of empirical research and relevant policy issues.

title: Cost-Benefit Analysis and Applications
officialDescription: Foundations and applications of cost-benefit analysis for evaluation of public policies relevant to environment, protection, health, economic development, and other public policies. Applications include data-driven assignments and analysis.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 5201 or equivalent with instructor consent. Not open for credit to students who have passed ARE 4464.

title: Industrial Organization: Empirical Analysis
officialDescription: Analysis of the structure, conduct, and performance of industries with examples from the food sector and other industries. Explains the development of testable hypotheses from theory, empirical methods, evidence on the level and type of competition, economies of size, product differentiation, entry barriers, and the impact of alternative organizational forms including cooperatives on economic performance.

title: International Trade and Policy
officialDescription: Analysis of international trade and trade policy focusing on agricultural and food markets. Covers trade-related issues concerning economic development and growth. Focus on current challenges to the multilateral trading system and the theoretical foundation for understanding the economic importance of firms, international trade, and global capital flows. Introduction of methods and tools for counterfactual evaluation of trade policies. Statistical modeling techniques to analyze trade patterns and measure trade policy effects.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 5201 or ECON 5201; ARE 5311 or ECON 5312 (or equivalents).

title: Effective Teaching Strategies and Course Design in Applied Economics
officialDescription: Introduction to course development and strategies for effective teaching. Students will be expected to attend teaching workshops, meet weekly with the instructor and their peers to discuss teaching-related topics, and work on developing their course materials including syllabi, course learning goals, lectures, and assessments.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to graduate students, instructor’s consent is required.

title: Special Topics
officialDescription: Topics and credits to be published prior to the registration period preceding the semester offerings.

title: Independent Study in Agricultural and Resource Economics
officialDescription: This course provides the opportunity for graduate students to carry on independent reading or research in the field of the student's needs and interests.

title: Valuing the Environment
officialDescription: Conceptual and practical understanding of main methods used to evaluate economic benefits of environmental protection and damages from degradation. Methods include: change in productivity, hedonic pricing, travel cost method, contingent valuation, defensive expenditures, replacement costs, and cost-of-illness. Topics covered include: recreation, soil-erosion, energy, forestry, hazardous waste, air pollution, deforestation, wetlands, wildlife, biodiversity, noise, visibility, water, and water pollution. Taught together with ARE 4438E.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 1150 or ECON 1200 or ECON 1201 or equivalent with instructor's consent. Students who have taken ARE 4438E cannot take ARE 5538 for credit.

title: Professional Internship
officialDescription: Professional or project based work in applied economics and policy related to agribusiness management, marketing and financial analysis, food systems, environmental and resource management, sustainability, or economic development. Requires a learning agreement and student's advisor approval.

title: Teaching Practicum in Applied Economics
officialDescription: Teaching practicum in the field of applied economics and policy related to agribusiness management, marketing and financial analysis, food systems, environmental and resource management, sustainability, economic development, and data analysis. Requires a learning agreement and student's advisor approval.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to graduate students.

title: Economics Methodology: Praxis and Practice
officialDescription: Philosophical foundations of economics as a science and economic research. Developing skills for planning, performing, reporting, and evaluating economic research. Critical thinking about the research process, reading about and discussing research methodology, analyzing the logic and reasoning of other economists’ research articles, and developing a research project.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Instructor consent; open to Ph.D. students in ARE (or Ph.D. students in Economics with Permission). Recommended preparation: One year of Ph.D. coursework in ARE (or Economics).

title: Applied Development Economics
officialDescription: Overview of the current applied literature on the microeconomics of development in poor countries, as well as examples from the US. Topics include the role of land policies, agriculture, human capital, health, education, the internal structure of households (neoclassical and bargaining) and the functioning of markets.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 5311 or ECON 5311 or equivalent. Recommended preparation: ARE 5201 or ECON 5201 or equivalent.

title: Applied Econometrics I: Regression Analysis for Causal Inference
officialDescription: Provides a rigorous foundation in applied econometrics with a focus on regression analysis for causal inference. Regression analysis helps address real-world problems beyond prediction, offering tools to examine causal relationships. Emphasizes both theoretical foundations - model assumptions, derivations, and identification strategies - and hands-on empirical data analysis. By the end of the course, students will be able to frame testable hypotheses, analyze complex real-world data, and apply econometric methods to inform research, policy, and data-driven business strategies.

title: Applied Econometrics II: Advanced Causal Inference
officialDescription: Econometric methods used in contemporary applied economic data analysis to examine causal relationships as well as machine learning techniques. Covered techniques include, but are not limited to, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, synthetic control methods, and causal forest. Emphasis in lecture will be placed on formulating identification strategies and implementing in standard statistical software (of the student's choosing).
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 6311 or instructor consent. Not open for credit to students who have passed ARE 5313.

title: Global Energy Transitions
officialDescription: Recent theoretical and empirical research on the economics of clean energy transitions from a global perspective. Topics include fossil fuel extraction, critical minerals and metals, renewable and green technologies, and challenges involved in decarbonizing electricity generation and consumption. Cross-cutting themes include energy poverty and development, industrial and climate policies, environmental impacts, and political economy. Focus on developing data-driven research and empirical estimation.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 5201 or ECON 5201 or ECON 6201 or equivalent graduate-level microeconomics course with instructor approval; ARE 5311 or ARE 6311 or ECON 5311 or ECON 6310 or equivalent graduate-level econometrics course with instructor approval Not open for credit to students who have passed ARE 5440.

title: Experimental Methods for Program Evaluation
officialDescription: Theory and practice of field-based program experiments, often referred to as randomized controlled trials (RCTs). All aspects of experimental program evaluation, including the design of evaluation strategy and working with survey and program staff. Examples from both developing country contexts and Western country program evaluation.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: A graduate level introduction to statistics or econometrics class or equivalent. Recommended preparation: A graduate level macroeconomic theory course.

title: Environmental Economics
officialDescription: (Also offered as ECON 6466.) Economic analysis of environmental problems and corrective policy instruments. Theory of externalities and public goods, role of uncertainty and imperfect information in policy design, benefit-cost analysis, and non-market valuation. Applications to environmental problems (such as air and water pollution, hazardous waste, and occupational health and safety).
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 5201 or ECON 5201.

title: Economics of Natural Resources
officialDescription: Economic concepts and issues related to the allocation of stock resources through time, the use and protection of flow resources, and the role of natural resources in economic growth.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 5201 or ECON 5201 or equivalent.

title: Applied Research in Environmental Economics
officialDescription: Designed for second year PhD students. Develops a broad perspective on the literature concerning the frontier areas of contemporary environmental economics, with an emphasis on empirical strategies for establishing causal relationships. Topics include: valuation of environmental quality and assets, evaluations of both private and public solutions to environmental problems, trade and the environment, environmental economics in developing countries, economics of climate change, and economics of automobile industry. Students will develop critical thinking skills evaluating published studies and identifying gaps in methodology and knowledge for future research.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 5201 or ECON 5201 or ECON 6201; ARE 6311 or ECON 6310; ARE 6313 or ECON 6311.

title: Microeconomic Applications to Food Markets
officialDescription: Trains students in applied microeconomics, with particular emphasis on food markets and public policy. The course is divided into three broad areas: production economics, economics of consumer behavior, and market analysis. Particular emphasis is placed on quantitative tools using empirical models and welfare economics. Students design and undertake an individualized project in their area of interest.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 5201 or ECON 5201 and ARE 5311 or ECON 5311.

title: Empirical Industrial Organization
officialDescription: Empirical Industrial Organization models that use simultaneous equations, discrete choice, and/or nonlinear econometric methods to analyze conduct and performance of brands and firms in noncompetitive industries. Includes static and dynamic modeling of pricing and advertising in differentiated product oligopolies. Antitrust policy applications in the U.S. and E.U.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: ARE 5201, ECON 5201, or equivalent. Recommended preparation: ECON 6201 or equivalent; ARE 6311, ECON 6310, or equivalent.

title: Graduate Research Seminar
officialDescription: Participation in research seminars presented by invited scholars and departmental faculty as well as active presentation of students' own research to colleagues and faculty.

title: Special Topics
officialDescription: May be repeated to a maximum of 12 credits with a change of topic. Topics and credits to be published prior to the registration period preceding the semester offerings.

title: Graduate Studio Art (Ceramics)
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: RC Art MFA students only

title: Graduate Studio Art (Painting)
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: RC Art MFA students only

title: Graduate Studio Art (Photography)
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: RC Art MFA students only

title: Graduate Studio Art (Printmaking)
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: RC Art MFA students only

title: Graduate Studio Art (Sculpture)
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: RC Art MFA students only

title: Graduate Studio Art (Drawing)
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: RC Art MFA students only

title: Graduate Studio Art (Video)
officialDescription: Open to students in studio art, others with permission.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: RC Art MFA students only

title: Graduate Studio Art (Performance)
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: RC Art MFA students only

title: Graduate Art Seminar
officialDescription: Discussions, readings, and analyses relating current studio work to contemporary trends in art.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: RC Art MFA students only

title: Issues in Art Criticism
officialDescription: Seminar investigating selected critical and theoretical issues of significance to the visual arts, involving a core of general reading and discussion on historical and contemporary topics in art from the 20th century to the present day. An individual research project culminating in an oral presentation and a final paper on the research are required.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: RC Art MFA students only

title: Interdisciplinary Study
officialDescription: Special course work that combines resources in art and/or areas outside of art.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: RC Art MFA students only

title: Studio Art Instruction and Curriculum Planning
officialDescription: Teaching methods, strategies, and curriculum planning in studio art instruction.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Must be taken in the second semester in the initial program year by all graduate students with teaching appointments.

title: Special Topics in Studio Art
officialDescription: Seminar focused on special, limited topic relating to practices in studio art. The content will vary from semester to semester.

title: Independent Study
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: RC Art MFA students only

title: M.F.A. Project
officialDescription: Seminar and studio work culminating in required exhibition, supported by a written statement, public presentation and photographic color-transparency portfolio.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: RC Art MFA students only

title: Curatorial Practices
officialDescription: Issues facing curators working in the arena of contemporary art today in a globalized art world.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to graduate students only.

title: Issues in Contemporary Art
officialDescription: Critical and theoretical issues in twentieth and twenty-first century art production and reception including modernism, postmodernism, feminism, technology, and globalization.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to graduate students in Studio Art and Art History, others with instructor consent.

title: Special Topics in Art History
officialDescription: Seminar focusing upon a special, limited topic in the history of art. The content will vary from semester to semester.

title: Independent Study
officialDescription: Independent study in Art History.

title: History and Theory of Digital Art
officialDescription: (Also offered as DMD 5670.) Investigation of forms of digital and Internet art and the forgotten histories of the technologies behind them. Forms of digital and Internet art to be explored include games/gaming, surveillance art, cyberfeminism, data visualization, and crowd sourced art, among others.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open to graduate students in the Master of Fine Arts, Digital Media and Design Master of Fine Arts, and Arts Administration Master of Fine Arts programs; others by permission, instructor consent required.

title: Statistics and Spreadsheet Modeling
officialDescription: Covers classical inference procedures and basic statistical concepts often essential to interpretation of business data. Students will learn to ask probing questions about the specifics of data and statistical techniques, to understand the conditions for drawing reliable inferences, and to assess the validity of statistical evidence. Topics include: discrete and continuous random variables, sampling, confidence intervals and hypothesis testing. Builds students' abilities for effective quantitative business analysis and communication, using a spreadsheet program such as Excel. Spreadsheet modeling uses such as regression, forecasting, simulation and decision models will be covered, in different functional areas including finance, marketing, operations, and management.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Not open for credit to students who have passed BADM 5180, 5181, or OPIM 5103.

title: Foundations of Economic Environments
officialDescription: Provides students with applied knowledge of key economic and psychological concepts that ground interactions among individuals and organizations in the global business environment.
prerequisites: Enrollment Requirements: Open only to MBA students, others with consent. Not open to students who have passed BLAW 5182.

title: Core Statistics
officialDescription: Covers classical inference procedures and basic statistical concepts often essential to interpretation of business data.
